newsitem.title: UK: Britain set for tax-cutting budget, report says.
newsitem.headline: Britain set for tax-cutting budget, report says.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke could cut taxes by around 3.0 billion pounds in his budget on November 26, a top business report published on Wednesday said.
The report, by the Institute for Fiscal Studies and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs, predicts the tax handout will be paid for by cuts in government spending plans for fiscal 1997-8.
But the report added that the tax cuts may prove unwise if the government is to achieve planned reductions in public borrowing.

"To cut taxes now in the expectation of hitting these medium term spending plans would be dangerous. And hitting these plans (for spending) would mean tough choices about the levels of state health and education provision," the report said.

Clarke has been under pressure from the right wing of the Conservative party to cut taxes sharply in November, to help close a 20-point plus gap in the opinion polls against the opposition Labour party.
But Clarke has been circumspect, arguing that voters would be "deeply suspicious" of large tax cuts because of broken promises on tax, made ahead of the 1992 election.
While 3.0 billion of tax cuts would be tolerated by British financial markets as relatively cautious, any more could spark a sharp sell-off, economists have said.

If Clarke wanted to cut taxes even more aggressively, the report says he could start to remove the tax advantages of Profit Related Pay (PRP). The scheme allows employees to pay less tax to the Inland Revenue if their companies hit certain profit targets.
"The cost of this tax relief (PRP) has grown rapidly, to an estimated 1.5 billion pounds. It is hard to defend, and clearly not achieving its stated objectives," the report said.

The IFS/Goldman report expects the budget to forecast the public sector borrowing requirement -- the gap between government spending and borrowing -- will drop to 21.7 billion pounds in 1997-8, 2.8 percent of GDP, and to zero by 1999-2000.
"If achieved this would represent a fiscal stance for the medium term which is broadly acceptable. But this relies on achieving unprecedentedly tight control of public spending," the report said.

In July, the government raised its forecast for the PSBR for 1996-7 to 26.9 billion pounds from a previous 22.5 billion forecast, and for 1997-8 to 23.1 billion pounds or 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The budget preview also warns that the government is likely to cut public investment plans to help finance tax cuts. "Although it would be particularly inappropriate to find spending reductions through postponing or cancelling public investment, that seems quite likely," it said.
Longer term, the report warns that there will be increasing pressure to trim government spending on health and education.

"The fundamental issue is how the objective of a declining share of public spending in GDP, or even a stable one, can be squared with maintaining the provision of these front line services at a level and standard which the public expects or needs. These are the choices no political party has really faced up to."
The report does not expect any substantial changes in company tax in the budget but notes the possibility of further cuts in the Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) rate in the future.
